danish.title: Syvende bog (1810–11) — Kapitel 9
paragraphs: Julen kom, og bortset fra den højtidelige messe, de kedsommelige julehilsner fra naboer og tjenestefolk, og de nye kjoler alle iførte sig, var der ingen særlige festligheder, selvom den stille frost på tyve grader Réaumur, den blændende sol om dagen og vinteraftenernes stjernehimmel syntes at kalde på en særlig fejring af årstiden.

Den tredje juledag, efter middagsmåltidet, spredte alle husets beboere sig ud i de forskellige værelser. Det var dagens kedeligste tidspunkt. Nikolaj, der om formiddagen havde besøgt naboer, sov på sofaen i dagligstuen. Den gamle greve hvilede sig i sit arbejdsværelse. Sonja sad i salonen ved det runde bord og kopierede et broderingsmønster. Grevinden lagde kabale. Nastasja Ivanovna, hofnarren, sad med et sørgeligt ansigt ved vinduet sammen med to gamle damer. Natasja kom ind i stuen, gik hen til Sonja, kiggede på hvad hun lavede, og gik så hen til sin mor og blev stående uden at sige noget.
»Hvorfor vandrer du rundt som en hjemløs?« spurgte moderen. »Hvad vil du?«
»Ham... jeg vil have ham... nu, i dette øjeblik! Jeg vil have ham!« sagde Natasja med strålende øjne og uden antydning af et smil.
Grevinden løftede hovedet og så opmærksomt på sin datter.
»Lad være med at se på mig, Mamma! Lad være; jeg bryder ud i gråd med det samme.«
»Sæt dig ned hos mig lidt,« sagde grevinden.
»Mamma, jeg vil have ham. Hvorfor skal jeg spildes sådan, Mamma?«
Hendes stemme knækkede, tårerne strømmede fra hendes øjne, og hun vendte sig hurtigt bort for at skjule dem og forlod stuen.

Hun passerede igennem dagligstuen, stod og tænkte sig om et øjeblik, og gik så ind i pigernes kammer. Der skændte en gammel tjenestepige på en ung pige, der stod og gispede efter at være løbet ind gennem kulden fra tyendekvarteret.
»Hold op med at lege — der er tid til alting,« sagde den gamle kone.
»Lad hende være i fred, Kondratjevna,« sagde Natasja. »Gå du, Mavrusjka, gå.«
Efter at have sluppet Mavrusjka fri krydsede Natasja dansesal og gik ud i forhallen. Der sad en gammel tjener og to unge og spillede kort. De afbrød spillet og rejste sig, da hun trådte ind.
»Hvad kan jeg stille op med dem?« tænkte Natasja.
»Åh, Nikita, gå venligst... hvor kan jeg sende ham hen?... Ja, gå ud i gården og hent et fjerkræ, en hane, og du, Misja, bring mig lidt havre.«
»Bare en smule havre?« sagde Misja muntert og beredvilligt.
»Gå, gå hurtigt,« opfordrede den gamle mand ham.
»Og du, Fjodor, hent mig et stykke kridt.«
Da hun passerede forbi anretterværelset, bad hun dem om at sætte samovaren over, selvom det slet ikke var tid til te.
Foka, hovmesteren, var det mest pirrelige menneske i huset. Natasja kunne godt lide at afprøve sin magt over ham. Han betvivlede ordren og spurgte, om samovaren virkelig var ønsket.
»Åh kære, sikken en ung dame!« sagde Foka og lod som om han rynkede panden ad Natasja.

Ingen i huset sendte folk omkring eller voldte dem så meget besvær som Natasja. Hun kunne ikke se mennesker uvirksomme uden at sende dem ud på et eller andet ærinde. Det var som om hun prøvede, om nogen af dem ville blive vrede eller sure på hende; men tjenestefolkene udførte ingens ordrer så beredvilligt som hendes. »Hvad kan jeg gøre, hvor kan jeg gå hen?« tænkte hun, mens hun langsomt gik ned ad gangen.
»Nastasja Ivanovna, hvad slags børn får jeg?« spurgte hun hofnarren, der kom imod hende i en kvindejakke.
»Lopper, fårekyllinger og græshopper,« svarede hofnarren.
»Åh Herre Gud, altid det samme! Åh, hvor skal jeg gå hen? Hvad skal jeg stille op med mig selv?« Og med klappende hæle løb hun hurtigt op ad trappen for at se Vogel og hans kone, der boede ovenpå.

To guvernanter sad hos Vogelerne ved et bord med tallerkener med rosiner, valnødder og mandler. Guvernanterne diskuterede, om det var billigere at bo i Moskva eller Odessa. Natasja satte sig, lyttede til deres snak med en alvorlig og eftertænksom mine, og rejste sig så igen.
»Øen Madagaskar,« sagde hun, »Ma-da-gas-kar,« gentog hun, idet hun tydeligt udtalte hver stavelse, og uden at svare Madame Schoss, der spurgte hende, hvad hun sagde, gik hun ud af stuen.
Hendes bror Petja var også ovenpå; sammen med sin tjener forberedte han fyrværkeri, der skulle affyres den aften.
»Petja! Petja!« råbte hun til ham. »Bær mig ned ad trappen.«
Petja kom løbende og tilbød hende sin ryg. Hun sprang op på den, slog armene om hans hals, og han galopperede af sted med hende.
»Nej, lad være... øen Madagaskar!« sagde hun, og hoppede ned fra hans ryg og gik nedenunder.

Efter så at sige at have inspiceret sit rige, afprøvet sin magt og forvisset sig om at alle var føjelige, men at det alligevel var kedeligt, begav Natasja sig ind i balsalen, tog sin guitar, satte sig i en mørk krog bag en reol og begyndte at lade fingrene løbe over bassens strenge, idet hun spillede en passage, hun huskede fra en opera, hun havde hørt i Petersborg med fyrst Andrej. Det, hun lokkede frem af guitaren, ville ikke have haft nogen mening for andre lyttere, men i hendes fantasi rejste sig en hel række af minder fra disse toner. Hun sad bag reolen med øjnene rettet mod en lysstribe, der slap ud fra spisekammerdøren, og lyttede til sig selv og grundede. Hun var i stemning til at dvæle ved fortiden.

Sonja passerede forbi spisekammeret med et glas i hånden. Natasja kiggede på hende og på revnen i spisekammerdøren, og det forekom hende, at hun huskede lyset falde igennem den revne engang før og Sonja passere forbi med et glas i hånden. »Ja, det var nøjagtig det samme,« tænkte Natasja.
»Sonja, hvad er det her?« råbte hun og anslog en tyk streng.
»Åh, er du der!« sagde Sonja med et sæt og kom nærmere og lyttede. »Det ved jeg ikke. Et uvejr?« vovede hun forsagt, bange for at tage fejl.

»Der! Det var lige præcis sådan hun blev forskrækket, og lige præcis sådan kom hun hen med et forsagt smil, da alt det her skete før,« tænkte Natasja, »og på nøjagtig samme måde tænkte jeg, at der manglede noget hos hende.«
»Nej, det er koret fra Vandbæreren, lyt!« Og Natasja sang melodien fra koret, så Sonja kunne fange den. »Hvor var du på vej hen?« spurgte hun.
»Hen for at skifte vandet i dette glas. Jeg er næsten færdig med mønsteret.«
»Du finder altid noget at lave, men jeg kan ikke,« sagde Natasja. »Og hvor er Nikolaj?«
»Han sover, tror jeg.«
»Sonja, gå ind og væk ham,« sagde Natasja. »Sig til ham, at jeg gerne vil have, at han kommer ud og synger.«

Hun sad et stykke tid og undrede sig over, hvad det mon betød, at alt dette var sket før, og uden at have løst dette problem, og uden overhovedet at fortryde, at hun ikke havde gjort det, gled hun igen i tankerne hen til den tid, da hun var sammen med ham, og han så på hende med en elskers øjne.

»Åh, bare han dog ville komme snart! Jeg er så bange for, at det aldrig sker! Og det værste af alt er, at jeg bliver gammel — det er det! Så vil der ikke længere være i mig, hvad der er nu. Men måske kommer han i dag, kommer med det samme. Måske er han allerede kommet og sidder i salonen. Måske kom han i går, og jeg har glemt det.« Hun rejste sig, lagde guitaren fra sig og gik ind i salonen.
Hele husholdningen — huslærere, guvernanter og gæster — sad allerede ved tebordet. Tjenestefolkene stod rundt om bordet — men fyrst Andrej var der ikke, og livet gik sin vante gang.
»Nå, der er hun!« sagde den gamle greve, da han så Natasja komme ind. »Nå, sæt dig ned hos mig.« Men Natasja blev hos sin mor og så sig omkring, som om hun ledte efter noget.
»Mamma!« mumlede hun, »giv mig ham, giv ham til mig, Mamma, hurtigt, hurtigt!« og igen havde hun svært ved at undertrykke sine hulk.

Hun satte sig ved bordet og lyttede til samtalen mellem de ældre og Nikolaj, der også var kommet til bordet. »Min Gud, min Gud! De samme ansigter, den samme snak, far der holder sin kop og puster på samme måde!« tænkte Natasja, og med rædsel mærkede hun en følelse af afsky stige op i hende mod hele husstanden, fordi de altid var de samme.
Efter teen gik Nikolaj, Sonja og Natasja ind i dagligstuen, til deres yndlingskrog, hvor deres mest fortrolige samtaler altid begyndte.

english.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Christmas came, and apart from the formal Mass, the solemn and tedious holiday congratulations from neighbors and servants, and the new outfits everyone wore, there were no special festivities — though the crisp frost of twenty degrees below, the dazzling sunshine by day, and the starlit winter nights seemed to call for some celebration.

On the third day of Christmas week, after the midday meal, the household dispersed to various rooms. It was the dullest time of day. Nicholas, who had been visiting neighbors that morning, was asleep on the sitting room sofa. The old count was resting in his study. Sonya sat in the drawing room at the round table, copying an embroidery pattern. The countess was playing solitaire. Nastasya Ivanovna the buffoon sat with a sad face by the window with two old ladies. Natasha came into the room, went up to Sonya, glanced at what she was doing, then went to her mother and stood there without speaking.
"Why are you wandering about like a lost soul?" asked her mother. "What do you want?"
"Him... I want him... right now, this minute! I want him!" said Natasha, her eyes glittering, without a trace of a smile.
The countess raised her head and looked at her daughter attentively.
"Don't look at me, Mama! Don't look — I'll burst into tears."
"Sit down here with me for a minute," said the countess.
"Mama, I want him. Why am I being wasted like this, Mama?"
Her voice broke, tears poured from her eyes, and she turned quickly to hide them and left the room.

She went into the sitting room, stood there thinking for a moment, and then walked into the servants' quarters. There an old maidservant was scolding a young girl who stood panting, having just run in from the cold outside.
"Stop playing around — there's a time for everything," said the old woman.
"Leave her alone, Kondratevna," said Natasha. "Go on, Mavrushka, go."
Having released Mavrushka, Natasha crossed the ballroom and went to the vestibule. There an old footman and two young ones were playing cards. They broke off and stood up when she entered.
"What can I do with them?" thought Natasha.
"Oh, Nikita, please go... where can I send him?... Yes, go to the yard and bring me a chicken — a rooster, please. And you, Misha, bring me some oats."
"Just a few oats?" said Misha, cheerfully and eagerly.
"Go, go quickly," the old man urged him.
"And you, Theodore, get me a piece of chalk."
Passing the butler's pantry on her way, she told them to set up the samovar, though it was not at all time for tea.
Foka, the butler, was the most ill-tempered person in the house. Natasha liked to test her power over him. He didn't trust the order and asked whether the samovar was really wanted.
"Oh dear, what a young lady!" said Foka, pretending to frown at Natasha.

No one in the house sent people running around or gave them as much trouble as Natasha did. She couldn't see people sitting idle without sending them off on some errand. She seemed to be testing whether any of them would get angry or sulky with her; but the servants carried out no one's orders as willingly as they did hers. "What can I do? Where can I go?" she thought, walking slowly down the corridor.
"Nastasya Ivanovna, what kind of children will I have?" she asked the buffoon, who was coming toward her in a woman's jacket.
"Why, fleas, crickets, grasshoppers," answered the buffoon.
"O Lord, O Lord, it's always the same! Oh, where am I to go? What am I to do with myself?" And tapping her heels, she ran quickly upstairs to see Vogel and his wife, who lived on the upper floor.

Two governesses were sitting with the Vogels at a table covered with plates of raisins, walnuts, and almonds. They were discussing whether it was cheaper to live in Moscow or Odessa. Natasha sat down, listened to their talk with a serious, thoughtful expression, and then got up again.

"The island of Madagascar," she said. "Ma-da-gas-car," she repeated, pronouncing each syllable distinctly, and without responding to Madame Schoss, who asked her what she was saying, she left the room.
Her brother Petya was also upstairs; with his personal attendant he was preparing fireworks to set off that night.
"Petya! Petya!" she called to him. "Carry me downstairs."
Petya ran up and offered her his back. She jumped on, throwing her arms around his neck, and he pranced along with her.
"No, stop... the island of Madagascar!" she said, and jumping off his back she went downstairs.

Having, as it were, reviewed her kingdom, tested her authority, and confirmed that everyone was obedient — yet found that it was still boring — Natasha went to the ballroom, picked up her guitar, sat down in a dark corner behind a bookcase, and began running her fingers over the bass strings, picking out a passage from an opera she had heard in Petersburg with Prince Andrew. What she produced from the guitar would have meant nothing to other listeners, but in her imagination a whole cascade of memories rose from those sounds. She sat behind the bookcase with her eyes fixed on a streak of light escaping from the pantry door and listened to herself and reflected. She was in a mood for dwelling on the past.

Sonya passed by the pantry with a glass in her hand. Natasha glanced at her and at the crack in the pantry door, and it seemed to her that she remembered the light falling through that crack once before, and Sonya passing with a glass in her hand. "Yes, it was exactly the same," thought Natasha.
"Sonya, what is this?" she called out, plucking a thick string.
"Oh, you're in here!" said Sonya with a start, and came closer to listen. "I don't know. A storm?" she ventured timidly, afraid of being wrong.
"There! That's exactly how she flinched, and how she came up smiling timidly when all this happened before," thought Natasha, "and in just the same way I thought there was something lacking in her."
"No, it's the chorus from The Water Carrier — listen!" And Natasha sang the chorus melody so Sonya could recognize it. "Where were you going?" she asked.
"To change the water in this glass. I'm just finishing the design."
"You always find something to keep you busy, but I can't," said Natasha. "And where's Nicholas?"
"Asleep, I think."
"Sonya, go wake him up," said Natasha. "Tell him I want him to come and sing."

She sat for a while, wondering what it meant that all of this had happened before, and without solving that puzzle or feeling any regret at not solving it, she let her mind drift back to the time when she was with him and he was looking at her with a lover's eyes.

"Oh, if only he would come soon! I'm so afraid it will never happen! And worst of all, I'm growing old — that's the thing! Then there won't be in me what there is now. But maybe he'll come today — come this very minute. Maybe he has already come and is sitting in the drawing room. Maybe he came yesterday and I've forgotten it." She got up, put down the guitar, and went to the drawing room.
All the household — tutors, governesses, guests — were already at the tea table. The servants stood around it. But Prince Andrew was not there, and life was going on as before.
"Ah, here she is!" said the old count when he saw Natasha come in. "Well, sit down by me." But Natasha stayed near her mother and glanced around as if looking for something.
"Mama!" she murmured. "Give him to me, give him, Mama — quickly, quickly!" and again she could barely hold back her sobs.

She sat down at the table and listened to the conversation between the elders and Nicholas, who had also come in. "My God, my God! The same faces, the same talk, Papa holding his cup and blowing the same way!" thought Natasha, feeling with horror a wave of revulsion rising in her toward the whole household, because they were always, always the same.
After tea, Nicholas, Sonya, and Natasha went to the sitting room, to their favorite corner where their most intimate conversations always took place.
